course: CSEG3060 — Research Methodology in Computer Science
assessment: Quiz 1 (Set B) — Unit I · Full Stack AI batches
instructions: 25 questions · 30 minutes · 25 marks (1 per question). This quiz does not test definitions — every question gives you a situation and asks you to diagnose it, exactly as the in-class drills did. Read each scenario fully before answering; the distractors are all things students actually say. There is no negative marking. Option order is randomised for every student, so comparing letters with a neighbour is meaningless. Your score is not shown at the end; results are released after the quiz.

questions.topic: I.1 — Task vs project vs research problem
questions.question: A team proposes: “We will build a RAG chatbot that answers student queries from the university handbook.” Which addition turns this from a project into a research problem?

options.A: Deploying it on the college domain with a proper CI/CD pipeline
options.B: Asking whether it answers a set of 200 real student queries more correctly than the existing keyword search, judged by staff-written reference answers
options.C: Switching the embedding model from a small one to a state-of-the-art one
options.D: Adding user authentication and a chat history feature

questions.explanation: A project's unknown is how to build it; a research problem's unknown is whether a claim holds. Only B introduces a baseline (keyword search), a population of queries, and a metric with a reference standard — the ingredients that make an outcome uncertain and therefore worth investigating.

questions.question: Which of these statements could NOT function as a research problem, because no possible result would make its author admit they were wrong?

options.A: Our microservice architecture is highly scalable and future-proof
options.B: Splitting the monolith into services raises p95 checkout latency under 500 concurrent users
options.C: Server-side rendering reduces time-to-interactive by more than 30% on 3G connections
options.D: Developers using an AI assistant introduce more security defects in authentication code

questions.explanation: “Highly scalable” and “future-proof” name no construct, no metric and no threshold, so no measurement could contradict them. B, C and D each state something that could come out the other way — which is exactly what makes them researchable.

questions.question: Four studies are proposed. Which one is design-oriented (constructive) rather than purely empirical or theoretical?

options.A: Measuring how five existing caching libraries perform on a fixed workload
options.B: Proving an upper bound on the number of messages a replication protocol requires
options.C: Building a new incremental build system and evaluating whether it meets a stated rebuild-time budget on real repositories
options.D: Surveying 200 developers about which caching library they prefer and why

questions.explanation: Design-oriented work produces an artefact that embodies a claim, then evaluates it against the problem it was built for. A is empirical, B is theoretical, D is empirical/qualitative. Only C constructs something new and tests whether it achieves a stated outcome.

questions.question: You find that a 2022 paper reports that aggressive prefetching improves API response times, while a 2023 paper on similar workloads reports that it makes them worse. Neither cites the other. Which source of research problems is this?

options.A: An explicit gap listed in a Future Work section
options.B: A contradiction in the literature that nobody has reconciled
options.C: An industry pain point published in a post-mortem
options.D: A replication study waiting to be repeated

questions.explanation: Two credible papers disagreeing, with no one reconciling them, is a contradiction gap. It is valuable because the reconciliation itself is a contribution: usually some hidden condition — workload shape, cache size, network profile — decides which result holds.

questions.question: Which of these is a legitimate and publicly available place to find real research problems that companies have not solved?

options.A: Marketing pages describing a product's key features
options.B: Public incident post-mortems and the “Limitations” pages of commercial API documentation
options.C: Job advertisements listing the technologies a company uses
options.D: Conference keynote videos summarising a company's achievements

questions.explanation: Companies publish their pain in post-mortems, issue trackers and the limitations sections of their docs — not in papers, and certainly not in marketing. Those documents state, in the company's own words, what does not yet work.

questions.question: A well-cited toxicity classifier was trained and validated entirely on English social media text. A student proposes evaluating it on Hindi–English code-mixed comments. Which kind of gap is being exploited?

options.A: A population gap — a method untested on a different group or setting
options.B: An assumption gap — something everyone believed and nobody tested
options.C: A contradiction gap — two papers reporting opposite findings
options.D: No gap at all — applying an existing model is not research

questions.explanation: This is the population gap, and it is the best-value source for a final-year project: the method exists, the metric exists, and the untested setting is one you have genuine access to. It yields novelty by new context, which is respectable and reachable.

questions.question: Applying the calibration rule — how many distinct final-year projects would satisfy this sentence? — which of these has been narrowed to roughly ONE project?

options.A: Large language models for education
options.B: Using LLMs to help students learn programming
options.C: Improving feedback quality in programming education using AI
options.D: For 60 first-year students, does LLM-generated feedback on failed test cases reduce time-to-fix below that of the compiler message alone, without lowering post-test scores?

questions.explanation: A is a field, B a topic, C still a topic wearing a verb. Only D names the population, the task, the comparison, the metrics and the setting — the point at which about one project fits the sentence and you can start work on Monday.

questions.question: Which statement is missing the single most commonly omitted element of a well-formed problem statement?

options.A: For low-end Android devices, does on-device inference reduce p95 latency compared with the cloud API, at equal accuracy?
options.B: Does quantisation to 4 bits reduce accuracy by more than 3 points on the same benchmark, compared with the FP16 model?
options.C: Does adding a vector cache cut median RAG response time relative to no cache, on our own query logs?
options.D: Does the new recommendation model improve engagement?

questions.explanation: A, B and C each name a comparison and a metric. D names neither a baseline nor a measurable definition of “engagement”, and no setting — it is the one that could describe a hundred different projects and be settled by none of them.

questions.question: Your plan evaluates 3 methods on 2 datasets, with 5 seeds each and 2 ablations. Using runs = methods × datasets × seeds × (1 + ablations), and 0.5 hours per run, how much compute does the plan need?

options.A: 30 runs — 15 hours
options.B: 60 runs — 30 hours
options.C: 90 runs — 45 hours
options.D: 180 runs — 90 hours

questions.explanation: 3 × 2 × 5 × (1 + 2) = 90 runs, at half an hour each = 45 hours. Students routinely under-estimate this by an order of magnitude, because the terms multiply — and because the first failed run is never the last.

questions.question: A problem scores well on every FINER + M row except Ethical, where it scores 1: it requires scraping personal profile data in violation of the site's terms of service. What is the correct response?

options.A: Narrow the scope to fewer profiles so less data is collected
options.B: Re-measure using a different metric on the same scraped data
options.C: Abandon this design — a hard ethics failure has only one move
options.D: Proceed, and declare the terms-of-service issue as a limitation

questions.explanation: The criteria multiply, so a 1 anywhere is fatal — and ethics is the one row with no repair. Scraping less data unlawfully is still unlawful; declaring it does not license it. Abandoning the design is not a defeat, it is a saved semester, and the research interest can often be re-anchored onto a consented corpus.

questions.topic: I.4 — Relevance and the so-what chain
questions.question: Which of these is “relevance theatre” — a justification that fits every project and therefore none?

options.A: If this works, an on-call engineer triages 60 alerts a shift instead of 100, so real incidents are seen on day one
options.B: If this works, the department can drop the paid API and save roughly ₹40,000 a year
options.C: This work will help society and contribute to the growth of the nation
options.D: If this holds, the library maintainers can change the default cache size with evidence behind it

questions.explanation: Run the so-what chain until somebody acts differently. A, B and D each end with a named person changing a decision. C ends nowhere — it could be pasted into any proposal in the university, which is exactly why it persuades nobody.

questions.question: Which of these correctly completes the chain construct → operational definition → metric → threshold for the construct “efficient”?

options.A: Efficient means the code is clean and well structured, measured by peer opinion
options.B: Efficient means inference on the target device, measured as p95 latency and peak RAM, with thresholds of under 100 ms and under 512 MB
options.C: Efficient means the model is smaller, measured by the number of parameters
options.D: Efficient means users are satisfied with the speed, measured by a five-point rating

questions.explanation: Only B names all four links, including the thresholds that decide success in advance. C measures a proxy that can shrink while latency worsens; A and D substitute opinion for the construct.

questions.question: A team writes: “We will apply a Graph Neural Network to our hostel mess attendance data.” Which repair addresses the actual error?

options.A: Narrow it to one hostel and one semester of data
options.B: Re-measure using accuracy instead of RMSE
options.C: Re-anchor to a real decision somebody makes — for example whether the warden can cut food waste by predicting evening attendance
options.D: Add a second model so there is a comparison

questions.explanation: This is method-first framing: the technique came first and the problem was reverse-engineered to fit it, so nobody changes anything if it works. The repair is to re-anchor on a person's pain and let the method follow — which also supplies a baseline, a threshold and a reason to care.

questions.question: A proposal promises a model that detects fake news with 99.9% accuracy across all languages and topics. What is the most likely explanation an experienced reviewer will reach for first?

options.A: The team has found a genuinely superior architecture
options.B: There is a leak or a trivially imbalanced test set producing the number
options.C: The problem is easier than the literature suggests
options.D: The team simply trained for more epochs than previous work

questions.explanation: If a result would make you extremely rich or overturn a well-tested body of work, the burden of proof is correspondingly high — and in practice such numbers come from leakage, duplicated data across splits, or a test set where one class dominates. The repair is to re-measure it as a validity or replication question.

questions.question: “AI for smart cities” is diagnosed as over-scoped. Which knob should be turned FIRST, and why?

options.A: The metric, because measurement is what makes a problem falsifiable
options.B: The population or setting, because that is where a student's novelty legitimately comes from
options.C: The method, because the choice of algorithm decides the contribution
options.D: The comparison, because reviewers care most about baselines

questions.explanation: All five knobs matter, but population is turned first because nobody else will have turned it the way you do — your city, your language, your device class, your users. That is novelty by new context, the most reachable kind for a final-year project.

questions.question: A team evaluates on five datasets and reports the one where their method wins. What is this, and what prevents it?

options.A: Sensible reporting; space in a paper is limited
options.B: Metric shopping, prevented by pre-committing dataset, metric and threshold in a dated notebook entry before running anything
options.C: An over-scoping error, prevented by narrowing to one dataset
options.D: A feasibility error, prevented by requesting more compute

questions.explanation: Selecting the dataset after seeing the results converts an exploratory finding into a claim that was never tested. The protection is procedural, not moral: fix the dataset, metric and threshold in advance, with a date, and report all five results.

questions.question: Which of these is a properly written delimitation?

options.A: We will not test on iOS devices
options.B: We may extend the study to iOS if time permits
options.C: We exclude iOS devices, because our instrumentation library has no iOS build and our question concerns Android memory behaviour, which iOS results would not inform
options.D: iOS devices are outside the scope of this study

questions.explanation: A delimitation is an exclusion you chose, carrying its reason and an argument that the exclusion does not damage the claim. A and D read as oversights, and B is not a boundary at all — it is the sentence that lets a project expand at 2 a.m. in week nine.

questions.question: Four specific objectives are listed for a twelve-week project. Which one is a wish rather than an objective?

options.A: Measure cold-start latency of the serverless endpoint across three memory settings (Figure 1)
options.B: Compare retrieval precision of BM25 and dense retrieval on 200 annotated queries (Table 2)
options.C: Explore the landscape of modern vector databases and gain familiarity with their trade-offs
options.D: Quantify the token-cost reduction achieved by response caching over one week of live traffic (Table 3)

questions.explanation: Each real objective maps to exactly one experiment and one table or figure. C produces no artefact, names no observable, and cannot be checked off by you or by an examiner — it belongs in the work plan as preparation, not in the objectives.

questions.question: When must a directional hypothesis and its refutation condition be written down?

options.A: Before running anything, with a date — so that the finding cannot be reshaped after the results are seen
options.B: After the first set of results, so the hypothesis reflects what the data actually shows
options.C: During the writing of the final report, once the story is clear
options.D: Only if a statistical test will be used

questions.explanation: Writing the hypothesis after seeing results is HARKing — it turns an exploratory observation into a confirmatory claim that was never tested. The dated, pre-committed entry in your notebook is what separates a finding from a story told afterwards.

questions.topic: I.6 — The chain from problem to claim
questions.question: A study measures p95 API latency before and after a rewrite, and concludes: “users find the new version more satisfying to use.” At which join does the chain break?

options.A: Problem → Question
options.B: Objectives → Hypotheses
options.C: Method → Data
options.D: Metric → Claim

questions.explanation: Latency is measured; satisfaction is claimed. The metric does not carry the construct in the conclusion — a construct-validity break at the last join. Either narrow the claim to latency, or add an instrument that actually measures satisfaction, such as task success and a validated questionnaire.

questions.question: A team wants to defend the claim: “An offline-first sync engine can keep a 50 MB dataset consistent across three devices on intermittent 2G, within a 200 ms merge budget.” Which investigative approach fits?

options.A: Analytical — the claim is universal and needs a proof
options.B: Design science — the claim is about buildability under stated constraints, so the artefact plus its evaluation is the evidence
options.C: Simulation only — no real devices should be involved
options.D: A questionnaire study with developers who have built sync engines

questions.explanation: “Can outcome O be achieved subject to constraints C₁ and C₂, and at what cost?” is the design-science claim form. The artefact embodies the claim; the evaluation must be capable of showing that the budget is not met.

questions.question: A final-year team submits a working system, a polished demo video, and screenshots of it succeeding on three examples they chose. What is missing, in research terms?

options.A: Nothing — a working artefact is the contribution
options.B: An evaluation that could have failed: a defined set of cases, a comparison, reported success and failure rates
options.C: A more attractive user interface for the demonstration
options.D: A larger training dataset for the underlying model

questions.explanation: A demonstration shows the artefact exists and cannot fail. An evaluation tests the claim the artefact embodies and could refute it — which means cases you did not choose, a comparison with current practice, and honest reporting of where it breaks. This is the single most common gap in B.Tech projects.

questions.question: A usability study recruits 25 students from the team's own hostel floor and concludes that “engineering students in India prefer the new dashboard.” Which validity is threatened, and what is the honest fix?

options.A: Internal — add more experimental controls to the session protocol
options.B: Construct — replace the preference measure with a different questionnaire
options.C: External — either narrow the claim to the population actually sampled, or declare convenience sampling as a limitation and state what it costs
options.D: Conclusion — apply a stronger statistical test to the same 25 responses

questions.explanation: This is external validity: a convenience sample from one floor of one hostel cannot support a national claim, and no statistical test repairs that. The fix is honesty about the population — either shrink the claim to fit the sample, or declare the sampling and its likely bias direction.

questions.question: A team standardises every numeric feature using the mean and standard deviation of the complete dataset, and then splits it into training and test sets. Why does this invalidate the reported accuracy?

options.A: It does not — standardisation is a required preprocessing step
options.B: Because information from the test set has already influenced training through the scaling statistics
options.C: Because standardisation should always be applied after model training
options.D: Because the mean and standard deviation are the wrong statistics for scaling

questions.explanation: This is preprocessing leakage. The scaler has seen the test data, so the test set is no longer untouched and the reported number is optimistic. Fit every transformation on the training split only — or inside each cross-validation fold — and always split first.

questions.question: Analysis of six months of repository data shows that pull requests reviewed within two hours have 40% fewer post-merge defects. Which sentence may the study honestly publish?

options.A: Fast code review causes a 40% reduction in post-merge defects
options.B: Teams should mandate two-hour review turnaround to cut defects by 40%
options.C: Rapid review time is associated with fewer post-merge defects; whether it causes the reduction would need a controlled intervention
options.D: Slow reviewers are responsible for most production defects

questions.explanation: Observational data licenses association, not causation — simple pull requests are both reviewed faster and less defect-prone, which alone could produce this pattern. Only a controlled intervention licenses a causal verb, and A, B and D all quietly assume one.
